power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Discarding the Razor, Ratifying the Drift: Identity-Protective Reasoning and the Institutional Entrenchment of Contested Certainties in Addiction Treatment and Policy

text.text: The addiction field is unusually rich in durable, contested certainties: that confrontation breaks through denial, that medication treatment merely substitutes one drug for another, that a single treatment philosophy fits all, or, conversely, that any criticism of a favored model reflects stigma rather than evidence.
This conceptual article introduces two linked constructs to explain how such certainties survive contrary evidence.

Occam's Disposable Razor (ODR) names a bounded micro-level event: the moment at which a simpler, coherent, evidence-consistent explanation is available and is nonetheless discarded because accepting it threatens identity, belonging, authority, safety, or an inherited narrative, with parsimony, noncontradiction, and falsifiability abandoned together.

Ratified Reality Drift (RRD) names the macro-level process by which the protected interpretation is repeated, institutionalized, and inherited as taken-for-granted reality within families, recovery communities, treatment organizations, and policy systems.

We distinguish the constructs from motivated reasoning, cognitive dissonance, belief perseverance, groupthink, and the normalization of deviance; specify a nine-stage coding frame with explicit criteria for an ODR attribution; and apply the framework symmetrically to patients, families, mutual-aid communities, clinicians, and institutions, including both critics and defenders of the brain disease model and of medications for opioid use disorder.

We separate defensive discarding from legitimate skepticism and from protected private meaning, address the risk that the construct could itself be weaponized, and derive eight falsifiable propositions with associated research designs.
The framework has not yet been tested empirically; its contribution is a symmetrical, testable research program for a familiar clinical intuition.
Everyone who works in or around addiction has watched the moment.

A family finally hears that the simplest account of a son's missing money, weight loss, and shuttered friendships is a return to heroin use, and reaches instead for an elaborate story about a demanding job.

A counselor with three decades of abstinence-based practice reads a synthesis of trial evidence on opioid agonist treatment and concludes, without engaging the findings, that the studies must reflect industry influence.
A researcher committed to a neurobiological account of addiction encounters population data on natural recovery (e.g., Kelly et al., 2017) and files them under exceptions.
text.formatted: A researcher committed to a neurobiological account of addiction encounters population data on natural recovery (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kelly et al., 2017)</ref> and files them under exceptions.

text.text: In each case a simpler, coherent, testable explanation was momentarily on the table, and in each case, it was set aside, not for want of intelligence or evidence, but because accepting it would have cost something: an identity, a membership, an authority, a livelihood, or a story a family has told itself for years.
The behavioral sciences possess ample vocabulary for the general tendency at work here.

Motivated reasoning describes the influence of directional goals on cognition (Kunda, 1990); identity-protective cognition describes reasoning organized around the defense of group membership (Kahan, 2013); and research on belief perseverance documents how conclusions can outlive their evidential support (Ross et al., 1975).
text.formatted: Motivated reasoning describes the influence of directional goals on cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Kunda, 1990)</ref>; identity-protective cognition describes reasoning organized around the defense of group membership <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Kahan, 2013)</ref>; and research on belief perseverance documents how conclusions can outlive their evidential support <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Ross et al., 1975)</ref>.

text.text: What literature lacks, we contend, is a bounded unit of analysis for the specific inflection point at which a person or institution, confronted with a simpler and evidence-consistent explanation, discards it in favor of a costlier protected narrative.
It also lacks a connected account of how that single act of discarding, repeated and rewarded, hardens into the settled common sense of a family, a fellowship, a profession, or a policy regime.
This article proposes two linked constructs, first formulated in prepublished papers by the second author (K. Kesling, 2026a Kesling, , 2026b) ) and developed here for the addiction field.
text.formatted: This article proposes two linked constructs, first formulated in prepublished papers by the second author (K. <ref type="bibr">Kesling, 2026a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Kesling, , 2026b) )</ref> and developed here for the addiction field.

text.text: The first, Occam's Disposable Razor (ODR), names the micro-level event: the identifiable moment when the razor of parsimony is not merely misapplied but thrown away, together with the companion disciplines of noncontradiction and falsifiability.

The second, Ratified Reality Drift (RRD), names the macro-level career of the interpretation thus protected: its repetition, its institutional ratification, and its eventual inheritance by newcomers as unremarkable truth.
The addiction field is an apt proving ground for both constructs, for three reasons.
Its clinical encounters routinely stage exactly the confrontation the ODR construct describes.

Its recovery pathways are, on the field's own best current theorizing, processes of social identity transition (Best et al., 2016), which places identity protection at the causal center rather than the periphery.
text.formatted: Its recovery pathways are, on the field's own best current theorizing, processes of social identity transition <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Best et al., 2016)</ref>, which places identity protection at the causal center rather than the periphery.

text.text: And its institutions (treatment programs, mutual-aid fellowships, professional bodies, and drug-policy regimes) have repeatedly sustained practice orthodoxies at odds with accumulated evidence, sometimes at documented cost to life (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine [NASEM], 2019; Wakeman & Rich, 2018).
text.formatted: And its institutions (treatment programs, mutual-aid fellowships, professional bodies, and drug-policy regimes) have repeatedly sustained practice orthodoxies at odds with accumulated evidence, sometimes at documented cost to life (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine [NASEM], 2019; <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Wakeman & Rich, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Our aim is deliberately symmetrical.
The framework is not an instrument for diagnosing error in patients, in 12-step members, in critics of medication, or in any other convenient outgroup.
Clinicians, researchers, harm-reduction advocates, and the authors of conceptual articles are equally eligible subjects of it.
The article proceeds as follows.
We first situate the constructs in the motivated-reasoning, philosophy-of-science, and correction literatures, taking care to calibrate claims to the current state of evidence.
We then define ODR, present a ninestage observable process model with explicit criteria for an ODR attribution, and develop RRD through social-constructionist and epistemic-injustice scholarship.
We next set the constructs against their closest neighbors and state what they add.
Three applications in the addiction field follow: clinical encounter, recovery identity, and institutional paradigms.
We then erect safeguards against misuse of the construct, derive eight falsifiable propositions, and consider limitations and rival explanations.

Motivated Reasoning and the Defense of Identity Kunda's (1990) canonical statement established that directional goals shape which beliefs people arrive at, but through ordinary cognitive machinery: biased memory search, selective recruitment of standards, and asymmetric scrutiny of congenial and uncongenial evidence.
text.formatted: Motivated Reasoning and the Defense of Identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Kunda's (1990)</ref> canonical statement established that directional goals shape which beliefs people arrive at, but through ordinary cognitive machinery: biased memory search, selective recruitment of standards, and asymmetric scrutiny of congenial and uncongenial evidence.

text.text: People do not believe whatever they wish; they believe what they can construct a justification for, and motivation governs the construction. Epley and Gilovich (2016) summarize the mechanics as a matter of differential standards: people ask whether they can believe a welcome conclusion but whether they must believe an unwelcome one. Kahan (2013) reported that such reasoning is often organized around the protection of group identity and, strikingly, that greater cognitive sophistication can amplify rather than dampen it, because able reasoners are better at constructing the required justifications, a finding that has since been contested (Tappin et al., 2021; see Proposition 4). Kim et al. (2020) argue that rational belief maintenance and nonrational discounting can produce indistinguishable behavior, so that the two must be told apart by process evidence, a caution our staged model takes seriously. Gershman (2019) supplies the formal bridge between this psychology and our first construct.

text.text: He shows that robustness to disconfirmation need not reflect motivated reasoning at all: within a Bayesian framework, a reasoner who can invoke ad hoc auxiliary hypotheses may rationally protect a central belief, because the auxiliaries absorb the blame for anomalous data and so function as what Lakatos (1970) called a protective belt.
text.formatted: He shows that robustness to disconfirmation need not reflect motivated reasoning at all: within a Bayesian framework, a reasoner who can invoke ad hoc auxiliary hypotheses may rationally protect a central belief, because the auxiliaries absorb the blame for anomalous data and so function as what <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Lakatos (1970)</ref> called a protective belt.

text.text: Lakatos's own criterion for when such protection has gone wrong is historical: a research program degenerates when its auxiliaries stop anticipating novel facts and merely accommodate known ones.
Neither account identifies the moment at which protection is switched on for reasons other than evidence.
What our framework adds is a specification of that moment, when a simpler rival explanation becomes locally available and identity-relevant, and of what is discarded in it.
Gershman's result also sets a standard the framework must meet.

Because protection by auxiliary hypotheses can be rational, an ODR attribution requires evidence that the auxiliaries were recruited in response to threat rather than evidence, a requirement the coding rule below makes explicit.

One important complication must be registered at the outset. Flores (2025) argues that identity-protective reasoning is not uniformly an epistemic vice: at the collective level it can support a division of cognitive labor in which groups test divergent beliefs, and for members of marginalized groups it can correct for the distortions that arise from taking ideologically skewed evidence at face value.

text.text: This defense matters for the addiction field, where the evidential environment surrounding people who use drugs has long been shaped by stigma and moralization (Room, 2005), the conditions under which Fricker's (2007) analysis of credibility deficits applies with most force.
text.formatted: This defense matters for the addiction field, where the evidential environment surrounding people who use drugs has long been shaped by stigma and moralization <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Room, 2005)</ref>, the conditions under which <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Fricker's (2007)</ref> analysis of credibility deficits applies with most force.

text.text: A person who uses drugs and discounts a clinician's catastrophizing prognosis, or a community that distrusts institutions that have long pathologized it, may be reasoning protectively and well.
Our construct is therefore not defined by the mere presence of identity motivation.

It is defined, as the following sections specify, by the conjunction of identity motivation with the discarding of a simpler explanation that is evidence-consistent, and with the abandonment of the disciplines that would allow the protected alternative to be tested.
The framework braids three normative traditions that psychological accounts of belief defense usually leave implicit.

The first is parsimony. Sober (2015) shows that appeals to simplicity are legitimate when they proxy for likelihood or predictive accuracy and illegitimate when they merely express taste, and a recent multi-author appraisal argues that parsimony is a weaker proxy for good models than often assumed and can mislead in complex domains (Dubova et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The first is parsimony. <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Sober (2015)</ref> shows that appeals to simplicity are legitimate when they proxy for likelihood or predictive accuracy and illegitimate when they merely express taste, and a recent multi-author appraisal argues that parsimony is a weaker proxy for good models than often assumed and can mislead in complex domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Dubova et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We embrace both cautions.
The construct does not assert that the simpler explanation is always true; addiction is a paradigm case of multifactorial causation (West & Brown, 2013).
text.formatted: The construct does not assert that the simpler explanation is always true; addiction is a paradigm case of multifactorial causation <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(West & Brown, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: It asserts something narrower: that when a simpler explanation is coherent, consistent with the available evidence, and locally adequate, its rejection specifically because of what accepting it would cost is an epistemically distinctive event.
Parsimony here functions as a tripwire for motivated addition, not as a metaphysical thesis that reality is simple.
Which explanation counts as simpler is not self-evident, and the holder of a protected narrative may experience it as the simple one.
To a counselor committed to abstinence, the claim that medication is just substitution feels like plain truth.
The framework therefore uses a relative criterion that can be assessed against the record rather than against anyone's intuition.

Following Sober's (2015) treatment of parsimony as a proxy for likelihood, an explanation is simpler in the relevant sense when, given the evidence available at the moment of decision, it accommodates that evidence with fewer ad hoc auxiliary assumptions, meaning assumptions that lack independent support and are introduced only to neutralize a specific piece of evidence.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Sober's (2015)</ref> treatment of parsimony as a proxy for likelihood, an explanation is simpler in the relevant sense when, given the evidence available at the moment of decision, it accommodates that evidence with fewer ad hoc auxiliary assumptions, meaning assumptions that lack independent support and are introduced only to neutralize a specific piece of evidence.

text.text: On this criterion the substitution claim is the more complex account, because sustaining it against mortality evidence (NASEM, 2019) requires auxiliaries (that the trials measured the wrong outcomes, that their funders biased them, that this patient differs from every trial participant) that are invoked for that purpose and supported by nothing else.
The judgment is made on the record and can be contested on the record.
The second guardrail is noncontradiction.

The protected narratives at issue characteristically require their holders to affirm incompatible propositions across contexts: that a program is evidence-based and that inconvenient evidence does not apply to it; that a loved one is fine and that nothing may be asked about how they are.
The third is falsifiability in Popper's (1963) methodological sense: not a demand that every belief be testable, but a discipline of specifying what would count against one's claim.
text.formatted: The third is falsifiability in <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Popper's (1963)</ref> methodological sense: not a demand that every belief be testable, but a discipline of specifying what would count against one's claim.

text.text: The distinctive signature of the event we describe is that the three guardrails are dropped together.

The simpler account is refused (parsimony), the incompatibilities of the protected account are tolerated (noncontradiction), and the protected account is rendered untestable by design (falsifiability).
Any one lapse is unremarkable; the conjunction, under identity threat, is the phenomenon.
A framework of this kind must be calibrated to the correction literature rather than to its folklore.

The claim that factual correction routinely backfires, strengthening the misperception it targets, has not survived systematic scrutiny. Wood and Porter (2019) found factual adherence rather than backfire across a large set of contentious items; Swire-Thompson et al. (2020) traced many apparent backfire findings to measurement and design artifacts; and Nyhan (2021) argues that the durability of misperceptions owes more to the fading of corrective effects and to the elite cues and group identities that sustain false beliefs than to corrections boomeranging.

(2020)</ref> traced many apparent backfire findings to measurement and design artifacts; and <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Nyhan (2021)</ref> argues that the durability of misperceptions owes more to the fading of corrective effects and to the elite cues and group identities that sustain false beliefs than to corrections boomeranging.

text.text: Accordingly, our framework does not predict that evidence typically makes things worse.

It predicts something more specific and more testable: that correction will be least effective, and auxiliary-hypothesis generation most florid, precisely where the corrected belief is load-bearing for identity or institutional position.

This is an interaction claim, not a universal backfire claim. Anglin (2019) offers a calibrating anchor: participants who evaluated belief-inconsistent evidence with evident bias nonetheless shifted their beliefs in its direction.

text.text: Resistance is not the default response to evidence; it is the exception the framework must explain.

We define Occam's Disposable Razor as follows: a bounded cognitive-social event in which an agent (individual or corporate), confronted with a simpler explanation that is coherent, consistent with the evidence available to the agent, and locally adequate to the phenomenon, rejects that explanation primarily because accepting it would threaten identity, belonging, authority, safety, or an inherited narrative, and in doing so suspends parsimony, noncontradiction, and falsifiability together.
Three features of the definition deserve emphasis.
First, availability: the simpler explanation must actually be on the table (presented, articulated, or demonstrably known), which distinguishes ODR from mere ignorance.

Second, primacy of threat: the rejection must be driven by appraised cost rather than by evidential objection; where a genuine evidential objection is offered and defended, the event is ordinary scientific or clinical disagreement, not ODR.
Third, conjunction: all three guardrails are dropped.
This is what separates the construct from its neighbors.
Motivated reasoning names a pervasive tendency; identity-protective cognition names a motive; belief perseverance names an outcome.
ODR names a moment, the instant a working tool is abandoned precisely when it would work, and a moment can be observed, coded, timed, and experimentally provoked in ways a tendency cannot.
Table 1 presents the staged process model.

text.text: The stages are sequential in the ideal type, but need not all be present in every episode; they are offered as a coding frame, each stage paired with the class of observable indicator that would evidence it in addiction-relevant settings and with its role in an ODR coding.
The model's value is operational.

It converts a fuzzy clinical intuition ("they are in denial"; "the committee would not hear it") into a shared vocabulary that allows two observers to locate an episode, disagree about a stage, and resolve the disagreement against a transcript.
Because not every stage must be present, the frame needs an explicit rule for when an episode counts as ODR.
An episode is coded as ODR only when five stages are documented on the record.
Stage 1 establishes availability: the simpler account was presented, articulated, or demonstrably known.
Stages 3 and 4 establish two guardrail lapses: a contradiction is tolerated rather than resolved, and no condition is named under which the protected account would be given up.

Stage 5 establishes threat, and it must be shown by markers on the record (explicit reference to role, funding, membership, family standing, or loyalty as the stakes) rather than inferred from the rejection itself, which would make the attribution circular.
Stage 6 establishes the parsimony lapse: auxiliary hypotheses are introduced in place of the adequate simpler account, without a defended evidential objection.
Stage 2 (momentary recognition) and Stage 7 (closure) strengthen coding but are not required, because both are often visible only in their behavioral residue.
Stages 8 and 9 are not part of the ODR event at all; they mark its entry into RRD.
Two clarifications forestall predictable objections.
The model does not claim that people consciously traverse the stages.
Nor does it presuppose that the discarded simpler explanation is correct.
It presupposes only that the explanation was evidentially adequate at the moment of rejection, which is an assessable property of the record, not of the future.
A single discarded razor is a psychological event.
Ratified Reality Drift begins when the protected interpretation leaves the individual and enters circulation.

We define RRD as the process by which an interpretation originally preserved through one or more ODR events is repeated, socially rewarded, institutionally adopted, and eventually inherited by people who never faced the original choice, for whom it arrives not as a defended position but as unremarkable reality.

The sociological machinery here is classical. Berger and Luckmann (1966) describe how habitualized actions become reciprocally typified and institutionalized, how institutions acquire legitimating theories, and how successive generations encounter the result as objective fact.

text.text: Ocasio (2023) extends the account across levels, tracing how micro-institutions emerge within organizations and are nested in higher-level institutional orders and emphasizing the committed networks of role practitioners that sustain them.

What RRD adds to this general machinery is a claim about input and selection: that a systematically important class of the interpretations that get institutionalized consists of those forged in identity defense, because such interpretations arrive already bundled with loyalty tests, insider vocabularies, and penalties for dissent, precisely the features that accelerate ratification.
An interpretation that survived because questioning it felt like betrayal will be transmitted with the betrayal-feeling attached.
Fricker (2007) supplies the second mechanism: the distribution of credibility.
Ratification is not only repetition; it is the differential assignment of authority to tell the story.
In addiction contexts, credibility economies are unusually explicit.

Lived-experience status can function as a credential that licenses some claims and disqualifies others; professional titles do the same in the opposite direction; and people currently using drugs are routinely subject to the credibility deficit Fricker calls testimonial injustice, their own accounts of their situation discounted in advance.

Stigma toward people who use drugs is pervasive (Room, 2005), and health professionals frequently regard patients with substance use disorders as manipulative or poorly motivated (van Boekel et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Stigma toward people who use drugs is pervasive <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Room, 2005)</ref>, and health professionals frequently regard patients with substance use disorders as manipulative or poorly motivated <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(van Boekel et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: RRD therefore predicts that protected interpretations will drift fastest where credibility is most unequally distributed, because the people best placed to voice the simpler explanation are the people least likely to be believed.
The drift terminus is worth marking.
At full ratification, the interpretation no longer needs defending because it is no longer experienced as an interpretation.

Program manuals state it; induction reproduces it; funding categories presuppose it; and a newcomer who articulates the original simpler explanation is not refuted but corrected, the way one corrects a spelling error.
It is at this terminus that the framework connects to documented harm.

Where an interpretation hostile to effective treatment has been ratified, for instance the construal of opioid agonist medication as "replacing one addiction with another," people die of the drift's consequences without any individual, at the end, discarding anything at all (NASEM, 2019; Wakeman & Rich, 2018).

text.text: In her account of the Challenger launch decision, anomalies that should have triggered concern were incrementally redefined as acceptable risk until the redefinition was simply how work was done.
RRD shares that terminus but differs in its input and its signature.

Its input is an interpretation forged in identity defense rather than an incrementally accepted technical anomaly, and it predicts that such interpretations are transmitted with loyalty markers and penalties for dissent attached, producing the defended-then-inherited archival trajectory of Proposition 8.

The residual contribution, then, consists of three claims that none of the neighbors makes jointly: that the discarding of an available, adequate explanation under identity threat is a bounded and codable event; that the event is marked by the joint suspension of three normative disciplines; and that interpretations preserved in this way enter a distinctive institutional career.
Each claim is exposed to test in the propositions below.
If they fail, the constructs should be absorbed into their parents.
The Clinical Encounter: "Denial" Reconsidered
The concept of denial has an ambivalent history in addiction treatment: indispensable as a description, disastrous as a warrant for confrontation.
The ODR construct recasts denial as a locatable event rather than a character trait.

On this reading, the patient who deflects the simplest account of their laboratory results is not exhibiting a defect of personality; they are, at an observable moment, appraising the simpler account as a threat to identity and belonging and paying a real epistemic price to keep a narrative that still organizes their life.
This reframing is consistent with the empirical trajectory of the field.
The confrontational style once justified by trait-denial performs poorly.

In a controlled comparison of therapist styles, the more the therapist confronted, the more the client drank a year later (Miller et al., 1993), and a review of four decades of outcome research found no evidence base for confrontational therapies and several signals of harm (White & Miller, 2007).

text.text: Motivational interviewing, by contrast, is built on the premise that direct assault on the protected narrative entrenches it and that change talk must be elicited rather than imposed, and it has a substantial evidence base (Lundahl et al., 2010; Miller & Rollnick, 2013).

text.text: In our vocabulary, motivational interviewing works in part because it lowers the identity price of the simpler explanation before asking anyone to accept it: it addresses Stage 5 of the model rather than colliding with Stage 6.
The construct applies with equal force across the desk.

Clinicians hold identity-laden narratives about their own efficacy, their program's philosophy, and their profession's authority, and the clinical literature on stigma shows that health professionals' regard for patients with substance use disorders is frequently low, with consequences for care quality (van Boekel et al., 2013).

text.text: A clinician who attributes every treatment failure to patient noncompliance has rendered their own practice unfalsifiable.

The model codes that blanket attribution as Stage 4, and where the simpler account was on the record (Stage 1), a contradiction is tolerated (Stage 3), the stakes are marked (Stage 5), and auxiliaries take the simpler account's place (Stage 6), the episode is no less an ODR event for occurring on the credentialed side of the encounter.
Even the field's language operates as ratification machinery.

Experimental evidence indicates that describing a person as a "substance abuser" rather than as "having a substance use disorder" shifts trained professionals toward punitive judgments (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010), a demonstration in miniature of how a ratified vocabulary carries a protected interpretation into the judgments of people who never chose it.

text.text: The social identity model of recovery holds that durable recovery is substantially a process of identity transition, accomplished through migration between social networks and the meaningful activities they sustain (Best et al., 2016; Dingle et al., 2015; Frings & Albery, 2015).

text.text: This body of work gives the present framework its most delicate application, because it entails that identity protection is not incidental to recovery but constitutive of it.

A recovery identity is precisely a narrative that must be defended for the person to stay well, and the fellowship that reinforces it is doing therapeutic work of demonstrable value (Kelly et al., 2020).

text.text: The framework therefore does not pathologize recovery identity.

It predicts, rather, a specific vulnerability at the community level: interpretations that have become identityconstitutive for a community recovery will be defended by ODR dynamics even where they conflict with evidence bearing on other people's recovery.
The clearest contemporary case is the construal, still audible in parts of the mutual-aid and treatment world, of agonist medications as incompatible with "real" recovery.

Under that construal, people using methadone or buprenorphine may be discouraged from full participation or from their medication itself, against strong evidence that these medications reduce mortality (NASEM, 2019).

In one cohort of patients beginning buprenorphine treatment, most attended Narcotics Anonymous meetings, only about a third of those attending disclosed their medication, and roughly a quarter of those who disclosed reported being encouraged to reduce or stop it, even though meeting attendance was itself associated with better treatment retention (Monico et al., 2015).

text.text: The model's stages are readily instantiated: the simpler explanation ("this person is in recovery and takes medication") is available; its acceptance threatens a boundary that has organized members' own transformation; auxiliary hypotheses proliferate; the claim is insulated from disconfirmation; and the interpretation is transmitted to newcomers as settled fact.
Symmetry cuts here too.

A harmreduction community for which opposition to abstinence frameworks has become identityconstitutive can ratify its own protected interpretations, discounting evidence of benefit from 12step participation (Kelly et al., 2020) with equal fluency.

text.text: Different shelter; same razor in the bin.
At the institutional scale, the framework engages the field's longest-running paradigm dispute.

The brain disease model of addiction was advanced in part as an anti-stigma and accessto-care strategy (McLellan et al., 2000; Volkow et al., 2016); its critics argue that its empirical promises are only partially fulfilled and its social benefits overstated (Hall et al., 2015; Heather, 2017), while social researchers have documented how addiction concepts themselves are made and remade by institutional practice (Fraser et al., 2014).

text.text: The present framework takes no side in that dispute, and this abstention is methodological rather than diplomatic: the framework's subject matter is not which model is true but how each camp handles the moment when the other camp's simpler explanation of a given finding becomes available. Kuhn (1962) taught that paradigm allegiance is never merely evidential; the present framework adds a codable account of the moments at which allegiance is purchased at the price of the guardrails.

text.text: A case worked shows how the coding applies to the defenders of a model, not only to its critics.

Population survey data indicate that roughly half of U.S. adults who report resolving a significant alcohol or drug problem did so without treatment, mutual help, or other recovery support (Kelly et al., 2017).

text.text: The simpler account available on that record is that many such problems resolve without following a chronic, relapsing course, so that the chronic-illness description fits treated populations more closely than the population as a whole.

A defender for whom the model secures funding, clinical legitimacy, and professional standing may instead reply that the people who resolved their problems were never truly addicted, that their selfreports are unreliable, or that their remission will prove temporary.
Each auxiliary may be true in particular cases.

The ODR question is whether any of them is offered with independent support or a specified test, and whether its proponent would accept the same reasoning if it were applied to trial data favoring their own position.
Where the auxiliaries arrive without either, and the stakes are visible on the record, the episode meets the coding rule.

The same rule applies without modification to a critic for whom opposition to the model has become an identity and who meets neuroscientific or treatment-response evidence with auxiliaries of the same kind.
Drug policy supplies the starkest institutional cases because the drift is documented against a body count.

The interpretation of agonist treatment as moral substitution rather than medicine was forged in identity-laden commitments (of drug-free treatment systems, of criminaljustice institutions, of communities organized around abstinence) and then ratified into regulation, insurance design, and correctional practice, such that access restrictions persisted long after the mortality evidence was in (NASEM, 2019; Wakeman & Rich, 2018).

text.text: By the terminus of the drift, officials enforcing the restrictions were not defending anything; they were administering reality as they had inherited it.

RRD names exactly this conversion of a defended interpretation into an administrative fact and directs empirical attention to the archival record of the conversion: the hearings, guidance documents, and training materials through which the protected interpretation shed its defenders and became furniture.
Drift can also be reversed, and reversals are where the framework is most exposed to test.

In the United States, office-based prescribing of buprenorphine for opioid use disorder required a separate federal waiver, under a framework created in 2000, until Congress eliminated the requirement in December 2022 (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 , 2022 , div. FF, § 1262).

text.text: The waiver's history, from its creation through successive revisions of its patient limits to its repeal, is exactly the kind of documentary record Proposition 8 requires.

The framework predicts that justification density in that record should have risen again during the contest over repeal, as an interpretation that had become furniture was forced once more to defend itself.
Institutional inertia predicts no such rise.
A construct of this kind invites predictable misuse.

Deployed as a rhetorical weapon, it would allow any disputant to code any resistance as "discarding the razor," converting a diagnostic instrument into an unfalsifiable insult: a butter knife waved as though it still had an edge.
Three fences are therefore built into the construct itself.
First, the availability and adequacy conditions are evidential, not rhetorical.

An ODR attribution requires showing, from the record, that a simpler explanation was present and evidentially adequate at the moment of rejection, that the threat was marked on the record, and that the rejection was not accompanied by a defended evidential objection.
Where those showings cannot be made, the attribution fails.
Second, the construct is self-applying by design.

Any research program built on it must include the reflexive case, the investigators' own handling of evidence unfriendly to the construct, among its objects; a literature that only ever finds ODR in its opponents would itself instantiate Stage 8 of Table 1.
Third, the framework distinguishes defensive discarding from legitimate skepticism.
Skepticism proposes a test; discarding forecloses one.

The critic who says "your trial population does not resemble my caseload, and here is the comparison that would settle it" has kept every guardrail; the critic who says "trials cannot capture what we do here" has dropped all three.
A final distinction protects something the framework has no business pathologizing.
The construct's own metaphor marks it: declining to shave is not the same as throwing the razor away.

A person may decline to apply parsimony to a conviction that claims no authority beyond their own life; what the framework names begins only when the tool is discarded, and others are then asked to treat the result as settled.
We therefore distinguish protected private meaning from protected public claims.

A bereaved parent's conviction that their child's final relapse was not the whole truth of them, a person in recovery's spiritual account of their own transformation, a faith commitment that no evidence could unseat these are unfalsifiable by design and unaffected by the framework, provided they claim authority only over the holder's own meaning.

The failure mode the framework names begins at the crossing, when a private conviction demands public immunity and the unfalsifiable narrative claims jurisdiction over another person's treatment options, a program's admission rules, or a policy's design.
Flores's (2025) defense of identity-protective reasoning marks the same border from the other side.

Protective reasoning that shields a marginalized standpoint against distorted evidence is doing epistemic work; protective reasoning that shields an institution's convenience against undistorted evidence is doing damage.
The construct's target is the second, and its conditions are written to keep it there.
The framework earns its keep only if it can be wrong.
The following propositions are stated so that null or contrary results would count against it.
Proposition 1.

Experimentally induced identity threat (for example, a threat manipulation versus a neutral control, administered to treatment staff before they evaluate evidence unfavorable to their program model) will increase rejection of an evidentially adequate simpler explanation, and a prior self-affirmation manipulation will attenuate that increase, a pattern testable in a 2 × 2 threat-by-affirmation design.
Proposition 2.

Within coded transcripts of clinical case conferences and mutual-aid business meetings, auxiliary-hypothesis density (Stage 6) will rise discontinuously after threatappraisal markers (Stage 5), rather than accumulating linearly with disagreement per se.
Proposition 3.
The three guardrail lapses will cluster.

Because their conjunction is part of the definition of ODR, this proposition is tested by coding the lapses independently of, and blind to, the threat and defense codes: among episodes that show threat markers and auxiliary proliferation, refusal of an adequate simpler account will co-occur with contradiction tolerance and falsifiability avoidance at rates above those observed in episodes of ordinary disagreement matched for topic and intensity.
Proposition 5.

Public commitment will moderately drift: individuals and organizations that have publicly staked their identity to an interpretation (position statements, branded treatment philosophies) will show slower belief revision in response to the same evidence than uncommitted counterparts, controlling for prior belief strength.
Proposition 6.
Consistent with Nyhan (2021) and Wood and Porter (2019), corrections will not generally backfire, but correction effectiveness will be inversely related to the identity load of the corrected belief.

text.text: The interaction, not the main effect, is the framework's prediction.
Proposition 7.

Credibility inequality will predict ratification speed: in comparative organizational data, protected interpretations will stabilize into policy fastest in settings where the people positioned to voice the simpler explanation (patients, peer workers, line staff) carry the largest testimonial deficits.
Proposition 8.

Archivally, ratified interpretations will show the predicted life course: identity-defensive origins (contested, heavily justified), a ratification phase (adoption into manuals, training, and regulation), and an inheritance phase in which justification density falls toward zero while compliance persists.
This is the documentary signature of an interpretation that no longer needs defending because it has become reality.
Where a ratified interpretation is later challenged, justification density should rise again.

Suitable designs are within reach of existing methods: vignette and affirmation experiments with professional samples; conversation-analytic and content-analytic coding of recorded case conferences against the Table 1 frame and its coding rule, with inter-rater reliability as the first hurdle; longitudinal comparison of organizations before and after evidence shocks such as the publication of major syntheses; and archival process-tracing of regulatory regimes for agonist treatment, for which the documentary record is unusually complete, including the U.S. buprenorphine waiver from its creation to its repeal.

text.text: Four limitations deserve candor.
First, construct redundancy is the objection the framework must answer most directly: is ODR anything more than motivated reasoning with a memorable name?
Table 2 concedes the overlap with each neighbor.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> concedes the overlap with each neighbor.

text.text: Our answer is that the construct's content lies in three restrictions the parent literature does not impose (the availability of a locally adequate simpler explanation, the conjunction of the three guardrail lapses, and the boundedness of the event) and in the linkage to a macro-process, RRD, that motivated-reasoning research does not attempt.
These restrictions are empirical hostages.

If guardrail lapses coded blind to threat do not cluster (Proposition 3), or if auxiliary density tracks disagreement rather than threat (Proposition 2), the construct collapses back into its parents and should be retired.

Second, measurement is genuinely hard: Stages 2 and 7 are inferential, deciding what counts as a Stage 5 threat marker requires coder judgment, and the coding frame will live or die by demonstrated reliability on real transcripts.

Third, the framework's normative components ("evidentially adequate," "primarily because of threat") import judgment, and judgment imports the coder's own commitments; the reflexivity requirement and the record-based criteria are disciplines, not solutions.
Fourth, the scholarship on which the framework draws is largely Anglophone and high-income in provenance, whereas both recovery pathways and credibility economies are culturally variable.
The drift mechanics may differ where treatment systems, families, and fellowships are configured differently, and the framework should travel as a hypothesis, not as an export.
Two rival explanations merit standing acknowledgment.

Simple institutional inertia, in which interpretations persist because change is costly rather than because anyone is defending them, will explain some of what RRD claims; the discriminating evidence is the archival life course of Proposition 8, since inertia predicts flat justification density while RRD predicts the defended-then-furniture trajectory.

Rational-updating accounts, on which apparent resistance reflects reasonable priors or credible auxiliaries (Gershman, 2019; Kim et al., 2020), will explain some individual episodes; the discriminating evidence is the threat-linked pattern predicted by Propositions 1, 2, and 6.

text.text: Where the rivals win, the framework should yield.
The addiction field does not suffer from a shortage of evidence; it suffers, recurrently, from a surplus of protected certainty.
This article has argued that protection has a locatable anatomy.

At the micro level, Occam's Disposable Razor names the bounded moment at which a simpler, adequate explanation is discarded because it costs too much to accept, and at which parsimony, noncontradiction, and falsifiability are dropped together.

At the macro level, Ratified Reality Drift names the career by which the interpretation thus protected is rewarded, institutionalized, and inherited until it is no longer recognizable as an interpretation at all.

The constructs are symmetrical by design, fenced against rhetorical misuse, respectful of the identity work that recovery genuinely requires and of the private meanings no evidence should be asked to arbitrate, and cashed out in eight propositions that could show them to be wrong.

If the framework survives that testing, it offers the field a shared vocabulary for its most expensive habit: throwing away the tool at the moment it works and then teaching the next generation that nothing was thrown.
